name: Who Works in AI
blurb:
The World Economic Forum published its Global Gender Gap Report 2026 on 16 September 2026, and its AI chapter is the most detailed public measurement of who holds which jobs in the AI economy. The underlying data comes from the LinkedIn Economic Graph Research Institute.

The finding is not that women are underrepresented in AI, which was already known. It is where in the value chain the representation sits. Women hold about 44.8 percent of data annotator roles, above their 41.4 percent share of non-AI occupations. In the roles that build and deploy the models, representation falls by more than half: 19.3 percent of AI engineers and 20.6 percent of machine learning engineers.

The pay dimension is what makes that a structural finding rather than a preference. In WEF's reading of LinkedIn's US analysis, data annotators, the AI role where women are best represented, are among the lowest paid AI roles, with midpoint posting pay below the median of non-AI occupations. The roles with the least representation are among the best paid.

Two limits are worth stating because the report states them. The firm-type and role-type estimates exclude China, which the report itself flags as a significant limitation given China's role in the AI ecosystem. And the figures are LinkedIn profile data, so they describe the population that maintains a LinkedIn profile rather than the whole labour market.

points.desc: Women hold about 44.8 percent of data annotator roles across 19 economies with available data, above their 41.4 percent share of non-AI occupations. Among AI engineers the share is 19.3 percent, and among machine learning engineers 20.6 percent. The gap is not uniform across AI work; it opens where models are built.
points.name: Representation falls along the value chain, not evenly

points.desc: WEF reports that in LinkedIn's US analysis, data annotators sit among the lowest paid AI roles, with midpoint job posting pay below the median of non-AI occupations. Representation and pay run in opposite directions across the AI workforce, which is why seniority alone does not describe where economic value sits.
points.name: The best represented AI role is among the lowest paid

points.desc: By firm type, women's representation is lowest in the physically intensive segments: 21.8 percent at computer vision and robotics firms and 22.7 percent at AI hardware firms. It rises through AI tech and platform firms at 30.1 percent and vertical application firms at 33.1 percent, to 34.0 percent at Big Tech firms in the AI supply chain and 35.2 percent at foundation model firms.
points.name: Hardware and robotics firms are furthest from parity

points.desc: Comparing firms with at least 10 percent concentration of AI talent against others, women account for 36.6 percent versus 44.8 percent of individual contributors, 34.1 percent versus 35.9 percent in mid-level management, and 25.3 percent versus 27.7 percent in top-level management. The AI sector is not simply reflecting the wider labour market; it sits below it at each level.
points.name: AI firms trail non-AI firms at every seniority level

points.desc: The number of people adding founder to a LinkedIn profile rose 60 percent between 2024 and 2025, and women's share among founders stayed static at 28 percent. Among founders holding AI engineering skills the gap is wider: 8.7 percent of female founders have them against 14.7 percent of male founders.
points.name: The founder surge did not change who founds

points.desc: The firm-type and role-type estimates do not include China, which the report flags as an important limitation given the country's significant role in the global AI ecosystem. Any reading of these figures as global should carry that caveat with it.
points.name: China is excluded, and the report says so

points.desc: The underlying source is the LinkedIn Economic Graph Research Institute, so the population measured is people who maintain a LinkedIn profile. That skews toward white collar, English language and higher income markets, which matters most for the data annotation figures, since much of that work is done through platforms and outsourcing arrangements that may not appear as LinkedIn employment at all.
points.name: The measurement is LinkedIn profiles, not the labour force

summary: The World Economic Forum measured the AI workforce for its Global Gender Gap Report 2026, using LinkedIn data. The finding is a gradient rather than a gap: women hold 44.8 percent of data annotator roles and 19.3 percent of AI engineer roles, and the annotator roles pay least.
